text: The Painted Cave Fire was a catastrophic wildfire that occurred in June 1990 in the Santa Ynez Mountains and the city of Santa Barbara, within Santa Barbara County, California. The fire began near Painted Cave at the intersection of Highway 154 (San Marcos Pass Road) and Painted Cave Road, burning 5,000 acres (20 km²), destroying 427 buildings, and resulting in two deaths. The Santa Barbara County Fire Department had already been dealing with a 3-alarm fire at the county dump, and at 6:02 p.m. on a Wednesday evening, they received a call for a brush fire on Highway 154 and Painted Cave Road. That day, temperatures reached an all-time record of 109°F (43°C), contributing to some of the worst sundowner winds ever recorded. The first engine arrived at 6:05 p.m. and encountered winds gusting over 40 miles per hour (64 km/h), with about 2 acres (0.81 ha) actively burning; less than 20 minutes later, the fire had advanced over 2 miles (3.2 km) and flames reached 70 feet (21 m) into the air. The fire spread into residential areas of Santa Barbara, fueled by sundowner winds, and jumped U.S. Route 101 at 7:42 p.m. Within less than two hours, it had traveled nearly 4 miles (6.4 km), destroying 430 structures and killing one person—making it the largest loss of structures since the Bel Air Fire of 1961. The state fire marshal described it as the "fastest-moving fire of its type ever in the United States." The two fatalities were Andrea Lang Gurka, age 37, who died while fleeing the flames along San Marcos Pass Road, and an unnamed state prisoner working as a firefighter. Investigators concluded the fire had been intentionally set; a suspect was identified in 1995 but not charged. Instead, Santa Barbara County sued the man, and in 2000, he was ordered to pay $2.75 million in damages.
